In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of sialic acid in the fusion process of respiratory syncytical virus (RSV).
the role of sialic acid in the fusion and infection processes of RSV.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neuraminidases enhance RSV infection of susceptible cells by removing SA from the surface of virions and thereby increasing the accessibility of the fusion protein for its receptor.

neuraminidases can increase fusion and infection by RSV by removing sialic acids from the viral surface, which in turn increases the efficiency of fusion between the virion envelope and the cell membrane.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuraminidases can enhance RSV fusion and infection by a mechanism that does not require the removal of negative charges.
removal of SA from RSV-infected or transfected cells enhances fusion and that this is due to the removal of a fusion-inhibiting factor, rather than the removal of a charge-repulsion factor.
neuraminidases enhance RSV infection by removing SA on virions, thereby facilitating the fusion of the virus with the cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SA on the surface of infected cells is an inhibitory factor that must be removed to allow efficient RSV infection.
SA removal from virions or infected cells increases fusion and infection by RSV.

neuraminidases are useful tools for enhancing fusion and infection of cells expressing viral glycoproteINS, and that the enhancement is not due to removal of negative charges, but is likely due to a more direct effect on the viral glycoprotein.
